Zero-Density Concentration for Dirichlet Polynomials

Eric Dubon Affiliation: ORCID: 0000-0003-3400-7756
September 2026
Abstract

We prove that broad families of finite Dirichlet sums exhibit deterministic concentration of normalized vertical zero density on a single line. The main result gives a general criterion under which the normalized Jessen potentials converge locally uniformly to a piecewise-linear convex function with a single corner. The associated normalized measures describing the distribution of real parts of zeros in vertical mean density then converge weakly to a Dirac mass. Thus, for each fixed truncation, zeros may occupy a nontrivial range of real parts, while asymptotically their normalized vertical density concentrates on one line.

The proof combines the finite Bohr lift with a translation-uniform anti-concentration estimate for isolated prime coordinates. We apply the criterion to partial sums of the Riemann zeta function, fixed Dirichlet LL-functions, and primitive holomorphic Hecke eigenforms of fixed level, trivial Dirichlet character, and without complex multiplication. The concentration line is Re⁡s=1/2\operatorname{Re}s=1/2 in the normalized setting and becomes Re⁡s=k/2\operatorname{Re}s=k/2 for the classical Fourier coefficients of a form of weight kk.

1 Introduction

Let

PN​(s)=∑n≤Nan​n−s,s=σ+i​t,P_{N}(s)=\sum_{n\leq N}a_{n}n^{-s},\qquad s=\sigma+it, (1)

be a finite Dirichlet sum with a1≠0a_{1}\neq 0. For each fixed NN, PNP_{N} is an exponential polynomial in the vertical variable. Its zeros may occupy a wide range of real parts, and a substantial literature has developed around their location, existence, density, and zero-free regions.

For the special case

ζN​(s)=∑n≤Nn−s,\zeta_{N}(s)=\sum_{n\leq N}n^{-s}, (2)

Montgomery studied the extreme right-hand zeros [17]; Borwein, Fee, Ferguson and van der Waall gave extensive numerical and structural information [4]; Gonek and Ledoan obtained zero-counting results and information on the distribution of real parts in finite-height rectangles [9]; and Mora proved that, for every sufficiently large fixed NN, the set of real parts of the zeros is dense throughout the corresponding critical strip [18]. These results show in particular that the support of the zero set of a fixed truncation can be much wider than any single distinguished vertical line.

The same circle of questions has been pursued for broader arithmetic Dirichlet polynomials. Ledoan, Roy and Zaharescu studied zero-free regions and zero counts for partial sums of Dedekind zeta functions of cyclotomic fields [15]. Roy and Vatwani developed zero-free regions and zero-density estimates for partial sums attached to multiplicative functions [21], and later proved sharp existence results for zeros of the corresponding Dirichlet polynomials [22]. In a complementary direction, the author used Bohr equivalence to prove density of attainable real parts for partial sums of the Dirichlet lambda, beta and eta functions [7]. Very recently, Kerr, Klurman and Thorner [14] proved that unusually large partial sums of Dirichlet coefficients can force low-lying zeros of the underlying infinite LL-function away from the critical line. Their zeros are zeros of L⁡(s,π)L(s,\pi) itself, whereas the present paper concerns zeros of the finite Dirichlet truncations.

There is also related work for modular forms with a different approximating object. Li, Roy and Zaharescu considered symmetrized approximations to Hecke LL-functions obtained by adjoining to a truncated Dirichlet series the dual term supplied by the functional equation [16]. Their approximants are structurally different from the raw truncations considered here, and their asymptotic regime couples the truncation parameter with the height.

The question addressed in this paper is instead the following: where does the normalized vertical density of zeros concentrate as the truncation length tends to infinity? The distinction between support and mass is essential. A family can have zeros with real parts dense throughout a large strip while an asymptotically negligible proportion of its vertical zero density lies away from one distinguished line.

For fixed NN, the relevant convex potential is the Jessen function

JPN​(σ)=limT→∞12​T​∫−TTlog⁡|PN​(σ+i​t)|​𝑑t.J_{P_{N}}(\sigma)=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^{T}\log|P_{N}(\sigma+it)|\,\mathrm{d}t. (3)

The existence of this mean follows from Jessen and Tornehave [12, Theorem 5], while its convexity follows from [12, Theorem 7]. Their Jensen formula for ordinary Dirichlet series[12, Theorem 31] identifies 12​π​JPN′′\frac{1}{2\pi}J_{P_{N}}^{\prime\prime}, in the sense of distributions, with the vertical zero-frequency measure. Recent work of Andersson [1] develops related mean-counting formulae for vertical limits of infinite Dirichlet series. Our setting is finite-dimensional and introduces the asymptotic parameter N→∞N\to\infty.

The novelty here is a limit theorem for the whole Jessen potential. Under an explicit isolated-prime hypothesis, the normalized potentials converge locally uniformly to a piecewise-linear function with one corner; the corresponding normalized zero-density measures converge to a single Dirac mass. For zeta and fixed Dirichlet LL-functions the limiting line is Re⁡s=1/2\operatorname{Re}s=1/2. The same line occurs for normalized holomorphic Hecke eigenvalues, while the classical Fourier-coefficient normalization moves it to Re⁡s=k/2\operatorname{Re}s=k/2.

The principal analytic input is a translation-uniform logarithmic anti-concentration estimate for sums of independent Steinhaus variables with comparable weights. More precisely, if Z1,…,ZmZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{m} are independent Steinhaus variables and b1,…,bm>0b_{1},\ldots,b_{m}>0 satisfy maxj⁡bj/minj⁡bj≤K\max_{j}b_{j}/\min_{j}b_{j}\leq K, then, uniformly in a∈ℂa\in\mathbb{C},

𝔼⁡(log⁡|a+∑j=1mbj​Zj|)≥12​log​∑j=1mbj2−CK.\mathbb{E}\left(\log\left|a+\sum_{j=1}^{m}b_{j}Z_{j}\right|\right)\geq\frac{1}{2}\log\sum_{j=1}^{m}b_{j}^{2}-C_{K}.

The uniformity in the translation is essential: after conditioning on the remaining coordinates of the finite Bohr torus, the isolated prime-coordinate block is translated by a complex value depending on those conditioned coordinates.

All density statements below use the Jessen mean-motion order of limits: for each fixed NN the height TT tends to infinity first, and only afterwards N→∞N\to\infty. No coupled (N,T)(N,T) limit is asserted. This is different from the finite-height regime studied, for example, by Gonek and Ledoan [9].

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 states the abstract zero-density concentration criterion and its three arithmetic applications. Sections 3–5 develop the Bohr–Jessen framework, prove the translation-uniform anti-concentration estimate, and establish the abstract criterion. Sections 6–8 verify its hypotheses for zeta partial sums, fixed Dirichlet LL-functions, and holomorphic Hecke eigenforms, respectively.

2 Main results

Let

MN:=max⁡{n≤N:an≠0}.M_{N}:=\max\{n\leq N:a_{n}\neq 0\}. (4)

When a1≠0a_{1}\neq 0, Proposition 3.7 below shows that JPN′′J_{P_{N}}^{\prime\prime} has total mass log⁡MN\log M_{N}. Recall also that a finite convex function on an open interval has monotone one-sided derivatives [20, Theorem 24.1]; consequently its distributional second derivative is a positive Radon measure, namely the Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure associated with its increasing derivative.

Definition 2.1 (Zero-density concentration).

Assume MN→∞M_{N}\to\infty. We say that the family {PN}\{P_{N}\} exhibits zero-density concentration on the line Re⁡s=α\operatorname{Re}s=\alpha if

νN:=1log⁡MN​JPN′′→wδα\nu_{N}:=\frac{1}{\log M_{N}}J_{P_{N}}^{\prime\prime}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{w}}\delta_{\alpha} (5)

weakly as probability measures on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

This definition has a direct zero-counting interpretation. By Jessen and Tornehave [12, Theorem 31], for every a<ba<b,

JPN′′​((a,b))2​π=limT→∞12​T#{ρ=β+iγ:PN(ρ)=0,a<β<b,|γ|<T},\frac{J_{P_{N}}^{\prime\prime}((a,b))}{2\pi}=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2T}\#\{\rho=\beta+i\gamma:P_{N}(\rho)=0,\ a<\beta<b,\ |\gamma|<T\}, (6)

where zeros are counted with multiplicity. Thus (5) means that asymptotically all normalized vertical zero density lies in every fixed neighborhood of the line Re⁡s=α\operatorname{Re}s=\alpha.

For PNP_{N} as in (1), normalize a1=1a_{1}=1 and set

EN​(σ):=∑n≤N|an|2​n−2​σ.E_{N}(\sigma):=\sum_{n\leq N}|a_{n}|^{2}n^{-2\sigma}. (7)
Theorem 2.2 (Isolated-prime zero-density criterion).

Let PN​(s)=∑n≤Nan​n−sP_{N}(s)=\sum_{n\leq N}a_{n}n^{-s} with a1=1a_{1}=1, and let MNM_{N} be given by (4). Suppose there exist α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} and subsets

𝒬N⊂{p​ prime:N/2<p≤N}\mathcal{Q}_{N}\subset\{p\text{ prime}:N/2<p\leq N\}

with #​𝒬N→∞\#\mathcal{Q}_{N}\to\infty such that:

  1. (H1)

    for every σ∈ℝ\sigma\in\mathbb{R},

    12​log⁡N​log⁡EN​(σ)⟶(α−σ)+;\frac{1}{2\log N}\log E_{N}(\sigma)\longrightarrow(\alpha-\sigma)_{+}; (8)
  2. (H2)

    for every compact interval I⊂(−∞,α)I\subset(-\infty,\alpha) there is KI≥1K_{I}\geq 1 such that, for all sufficiently large NN, all σ∈I\sigma\in I, and all p,q∈𝒬Np,q\in\mathcal{Q}_{N},

    KI−1≤|ap|​p−σ|aq|​q−σ≤KI,K_{I}^{-1}\leq\frac{|a_{p}|p^{-\sigma}}{|a_{q}|q^{-\sigma}}\leq K_{I}, (9)

    and, with

    BN​(σ):=∑p∈𝒬N|ap|2​p−2​σ,B_{N}(\sigma):=\sum_{p\in\mathcal{Q}_{N}}|a_{p}|^{2}p^{-2\sigma}, (10)

    one has

    12​log⁡N​log⁡BN​(σ)⟶α−σ\frac{1}{2\log N}\log B_{N}(\sigma)\longrightarrow\alpha-\sigma (11)

    locally uniformly on (−∞,α)(-\infty,\alpha).

Then

JPN​(σ)log⁡N⟶(α−σ)+\frac{J_{P_{N}}(\sigma)}{\log N}\longrightarrow(\alpha-\sigma)_{+} (12)

locally uniformly on ℝ\mathbb{R}, and

1log⁡MN​JPN′′→wδα.\frac{1}{\log M_{N}}J_{P_{N}}^{\prime\prime}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{w}}\delta_{\alpha}. (13)

In particular, the normalized vertical zero density concentrates on the line Re⁡s=α\operatorname{Re}s=\alpha.

Remark 2.3.

The criterion is not intrinsically restricted to the arithmetic families considered below. Its application to further families reduces to two arithmetic inputs: the quadratic-energy asymptotic in hypothesis (H1), and a sufficiently large family of isolated primes on which the normalized prime coefficients are bounded above and away from zero, as required in hypothesis (H2). A suitable Sato–Tate-type equidistribution theorem provides a natural mechanism for the latter condition.

Theorem 2.4 (Riemann zeta partial sums).

For

ζN​(s)=∑n≤Nn−s,\zeta_{N}(s)=\sum_{n\leq N}n^{-s},

let JNJ_{N} denote its Jessen function. Then

JN​(σ)log⁡N⟶(12−σ)+\frac{J_{N}(\sigma)}{\log N}\longrightarrow\left(\frac{1}{2}-\sigma\right)_{+} (14)

locally uniformly on ℝ\mathbb{R}, and

1log⁡N​JN′′→wδ1/2.\frac{1}{\log N}J_{N}^{\prime\prime}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{w}}\delta_{1/2}. (15)
Theorem 2.5 (Dirichlet LL-functions).

Let χ\chi be a fixed Dirichlet character modulo qq, and put

LN​(s,χ)=∑n≤Nχ⁡(n)​n−s.L_{N}(s,\chi)=\sum_{n\leq N}\chi(n)n^{-s}.

Let JN,χJ_{N,\chi} be its Jessen function and

MN,χ=max⁡{n≤N:(n,q)=1}.M_{N,\chi}=\max\{n\leq N:(n,q)=1\}.

Then

JN,χ​(σ)log⁡N⟶(12−σ)+\frac{J_{N,\chi}(\sigma)}{\log N}\longrightarrow\left(\frac{1}{2}-\sigma\right)_{+} (16)

locally uniformly on ℝ\mathbb{R}, and

1log⁡MN,χ​JN,χ′′→wδ1/2.\frac{1}{\log M_{N,\chi}}J_{N,\chi}^{\prime\prime}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{w}}\delta_{1/2}. (17)

For the modular application, let ff be a fixed normalized primitive holomorphic Hecke eigenform of even weight k≥2k\geq 2, fixed level QQ, and trivial Dirichlet character; see, for example, Iwaniec [11, Sections 6.6–6.8] for the theory and normalization of newforms. Thus ff has a Fourier expansion at the cusp infinity of the form

f⁡(z)=∑n≥1af​(n)​e2​π​i​n​z,af​(1)=1,f(z)=\sum_{n\geq 1}a_{f}(n)e^{2\pi inz},\qquad a_{f}(1)=1, (18)

where af​(n)a_{f}(n) denotes the nnth Fourier coefficient of ff.

We further assume that ff has no complex multiplication. This is the hypothesis under which the Sato–Tate equidistribution theorem used below applies; see Barnet-Lamb, Gee and Geraghty [2, Corollary 7.1.7].

Define the normalized Hecke eigenvalues by

λf(n):=af(n)n−(k−1)/2.\lambda_{f}(n):=a_{f}(n)n^{-(k-1)/2}. (19)

With this normalization, the associated LL-function is centered at Re⁡s=1/2\operatorname{Re}s=1/2.

Theorem 2.6 (Fixed-level holomorphic Hecke eigenforms).

With ff as above, define

LN​(s,f)=∑n≤Nλf​(n)​n−s.L_{N}(s,f)=\sum_{n\leq N}\lambda_{f}(n)n^{-s}. (20)

Then the Jessen functions JN,fJ_{N,f} satisfy

JN,f​(σ)log⁡N⟶(12−σ)+\frac{J_{N,f}(\sigma)}{\log N}\longrightarrow\left(\frac{1}{2}-\sigma\right)_{+} (21)

locally uniformly on ℝ\mathbb{R}, and

1log⁡MN,f​JN,f′′→wδ1/2,\frac{1}{\log M_{N,f}}J_{N,f}^{\prime\prime}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{w}}\delta_{1/2}, (22)

where MN,f:=max⁡{n≤N:λf​(n)≠0}M_{N,f}:=\max\{n\leq N:\lambda_{f}(n)\neq 0\}.

Equivalently, for the classical Fourier-coefficient truncations

ℒN​(s,f)=∑n≤Naf​(n)​n−s,\mathcal{L}_{N}(s,f)=\sum_{n\leq N}a_{f}(n)n^{-s}, (23)

zero-density concentration occurs on the line

Re⁡s=k2.\operatorname{Re}s=\frac{k}{2}. (24)

3 Bohr–Jessen framework and zero-density measures

3.1 Finite Bohr lifts

Fix N≥2N\geq 2, let p1<⋯<pd≤Np_{1}<\cdots<p_{d}\leq N be the primes up to NN, d=π⁡(N)d=\pi(N) and write

n=∏j=1dpjvpj​(n),𝐯⁡(n):=(vp1​(n),…,vpd​(n))∈ℕ0d.n=\prod_{j=1}^{d}p_{j}^{v_{p_{j}}(n)},\qquad\mathbf{v}(n):=(v_{p_{1}}(n),\ldots,v_{p_{d}}(n))\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{d}. (25)

For z=(z1,…,zd)∈𝕋dz=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{d})\in\mathbb{T}^{d}, define the Bohr lift

FPN(σ,z):=∑n≤Nann−σz𝐯⁡(n),z𝐦:=z1m1⋯zdmd.F_{P_{N}}(\sigma,z):=\sum_{n\leq N}a_{n}n^{-\sigma}z^{\mathbf{v}(n)},\qquad z^{\mathbf{m}}:=z_{1}^{m_{1}}\cdots z_{d}^{m_{d}}. (26)

Then

FPN​(σ,(p1−i​t,…,pd−i​t))=PN​(σ+i​t).F_{P_{N}}\bigl(\sigma,(p_{1}^{-it},\ldots,p_{d}^{-it})\bigr)=P_{N}(\sigma+it). (27)

The elementary arithmetic fact behind the full-torus model is worth isolating.

Proposition 3.1 (Prime-frequency injectivity).

Let

ωN=(log⁡p1,…,log⁡pd).\omega_{N}=(\log p_{1},\ldots,\log p_{d}).

Then the resonance lattice

ΛN:={𝐤∈ℤd:⟨𝐤,ωN⟩=0}\Lambda_{N}:=\{\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}:\langle\mathbf{k},\omega_{N}\rangle=0\}

is trivial. Consequently the Kronecker orbit

t⟼(p1−i​t,…,pd−i​t)t\longmapsto(p_{1}^{-it},\ldots,p_{d}^{-it})

is dense in 𝕋d\mathbb{T}^{d}, and the map n↦𝐯⁡(n)n\mapsto\mathbf{v}(n) is injective.

Proof.

If 𝐤=(k1,…,kd)∈ΛN\mathbf{k}=(k_{1},\ldots,k_{d})\in\Lambda_{N}, then

0=∑j=1dkj​log⁡pj=log⁡(∏j=1dpjkj).0=\sum_{j=1}^{d}k_{j}\log p_{j}=\log\left(\prod_{j=1}^{d}p_{j}^{k_{j}}\right).

Hence ∏jpjkj=1\prod_{j}p_{j}^{k_{j}}=1. Unique factorization in ℤ\mathbb{Z} forces kj=0k_{j}=0 for every jj, so ΛN={0}\Lambda_{N}=\{0\}. The continuous Kronecker–Weyl theorem then implies that the orbit is uniformly distributed, and in particular dense, in the full torus; see Haviland and Wintner [10]. Jessen and Tornehave use this finite-integral-base torus representation in their spatial-extension construction [12, §116]. Finally, 𝐯⁡(m)=𝐯⁡(n)\mathbf{v}(m)=\mathbf{v}(n) implies m=nm=n by unique factorization. ∎

3.2 The exact Bohr–Jessen identity

At a zero of FPN​(σ,⋅)F_{P_{N}}(\sigma,\cdot) one has log⁡|FPN|=−∞\log|F_{P_{N}}|=-\infty. Thus the logarithm is neither continuous nor bounded on the torus, so the continuous Kronecker–Weyl theorem invoked above cannot be applied to it directly. We first record the required logarithmic integrability.

Lemma 3.2.

If QQ is a nonzero complex polynomial in dd variables, then

log⁡|Q|∈L1​(𝕋d).\log|Q|\in L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}).
Proof.

This is the standard finiteness statement underlying logarithmic Mahler measure; compare Boyd [3, Section 1]. We include the argument because the integrability near the zero set will be used below. Multiplication by a monomial does not change the modulus on 𝕋d\mathbb{T}^{d}, so it is enough to consider an ordinary polynomial.

For d=1d=1, write

Q⁡(z)=c​∏j=1r(z−αj).Q(z)=c\prod_{j=1}^{r}(z-\alpha_{j}).

Since QQ is continuous on 𝕋\mathbb{T}, the positive part log+⁡|Q|\log^{+}|Q| is bounded. It remains to check each factor in the negative part.
If |α|≠1|\alpha|\neq 1, then

infθ∈[0,2​π]|ei​θ−α|>0,\inf_{\theta\in[0,2\pi]}|e^{i\theta}-\alpha|>0,

so log⁡|ei​θ−α|\log|e^{i\theta}-\alpha| is bounded.
If |α|=1|\alpha|=1, write α=ei​θ0\alpha=e^{i\theta_{0}}. Then

|ei​θ−ei​θ0|=2​|sin⁡θ−θ02|.|e^{i\theta}-e^{i\theta_{0}}|=2\left|\sin\frac{\theta-\theta_{0}}{2}\right|. (28)

For |θ−θ0|≤1|\theta-\theta_{0}|\leq 1, the elementary bounds c1​|u|≤|sin⁡u|≤|u|c_{1}|u|\leq|\sin u|\leq|u| give

c2​|θ−θ0|≤|ei​θ−ei​θ0|≤|θ−θ0|.c_{2}|\theta-\theta_{0}|\leq|e^{i\theta}-e^{i\theta_{0}}|\leq|\theta-\theta_{0}|.

Consequently the only possible singularity is logarithmic, and

∫0δ|log⁡u|𝑑u=δ⁡(1−log⁡δ)<∞(0<δ<1).\int_{0}^{\delta}|\log u|\,\mathrm{d}u=\delta(1-\log\delta)<\infty\qquad(0<\delta<1). (29)

Hence log⁡|Q|∈L1​(𝕋)\log|Q|\in L^{1}(\mathbb{T}).

Assume now that the assertion holds in d−1d-1 variables. Regard QQ as a polynomial in the last variable zdz_{d}, with coefficients depending polynomially on the remaining variables z′=(z1,…,zd−1)z^{\prime}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{d-1}):

Q⁡(z′,zd)=∑j=0mQj​(z′)​zdj,z′∈𝕋d−1,Q(z^{\prime},z_{d})=\sum_{j=0}^{m}Q_{j}(z^{\prime})z_{d}^{j},\qquad z^{\prime}\in\mathbb{T}^{d-1},

For every z′z^{\prime} outside that null set, factor

Q⁡(z′,zd)=Qm​(z′)​∏j=1m(zd−αj​(z′)).Q(z^{\prime},z_{d})=Q_{m}(z^{\prime})\prod_{j=1}^{m}(z_{d}-\alpha_{j}(z^{\prime})).

L⁡(z′)\displaystyle L(z^{\prime}) :=∫𝕋log⁡|Q⁡(z′,zd)|​𝑑m​(zd)\displaystyle:=\int_{\mathbb{T}}\log|Q(z^{\prime},z_{d})|\,\mathrm{d}m(z_{d})

<∞.\displaystyle<\infty.

Proposition 3.3 (Bohr–Jessen identity).

For every fixed NN and every σ∈ℝ\sigma\in\mathbb{R}, the limit

JPN​(σ)=limT→∞12​T​∫−TTlog⁡|PN​(σ+i​t)|​𝑑tJ_{P_{N}}(\sigma)=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^{T}\log|P_{N}(\sigma+it)|\,\mathrm{d}t (31)

exists and

JPN​(σ)=∫𝕋dlog⁡|FPN​(σ,z)|​d​md​(z),J_{P_{N}}(\sigma)=\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\log|F_{P_{N}}(\sigma,z)|\,\mathrm{d}m_{d}(z), (32)

where mdm_{d} is normalized Haar measure on 𝕋d\mathbb{T}^{d}. Moreover JPNJ_{P_{N}} is finite and convex on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

Proof.

The frequencies −log⁡n-\log n are integral combinations of the finite basis −log⁡p1,…,−log⁡pd-\log p_{1},\ldots,-\log p_{d}. Jessen and Tornehave [12, Theorem 5] show that, for a nonzero analytic almost periodic function, the logarithmic mean exists and is obtained by first truncating the logarithm from below and then letting the truncation level tend to zero.

Fix ε>0\varepsilon>0 and set

gσ,ε​(z):=log⁡max⁡{|FPN​(σ,z)|,ε},z∈𝕋d.g_{\sigma,\varepsilon}(z):=\log\max\{|F_{P_{N}}(\sigma,z)|,\varepsilon\},\qquad z\in\mathbb{T}^{d}.

This is continuous on 𝕋d\mathbb{T}^{d}. Define

ΦN:ℝ⟶𝕋d,ΦN​(t):=(p1−i​t,…,pd−i​t).\Phi_{N}:\mathbb{R}\longrightarrow\mathbb{T}^{d},\qquad\Phi_{N}(t):=(p_{1}^{-it},\ldots,p_{d}^{-it}).

By (27),

gσ,ε​(ΦN​(t))=log⁡max⁡{|PN​(σ+i​t)|,ε}.g_{\sigma,\varepsilon}(\Phi_{N}(t))=\log\max\{|P_{N}(\sigma+it)|,\varepsilon\}.

Proposition 3.1 and the Kronecker–Weyl theorem therefore give

limT→∞12​T​∫−TTlog⁡max⁡{|PN​(σ+i​t)|,ε}​𝑑t\displaystyle\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^{T}\log\max\{|P_{N}(\sigma+it)|,\varepsilon\}\,\mathrm{d}t
=limT→∞12​T​∫−TTgσ,ε​(ΦN​(t))​𝑑t\displaystyle\quad=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^{T}g_{\sigma,\varepsilon}(\Phi_{N}(t))\,\mathrm{d}t
=∫𝕋dgσ,ε​(z)​d​md​(z)\displaystyle\quad=\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}g_{\sigma,\varepsilon}(z)\,\mathrm{d}m_{d}(z)
=∫𝕋dlog⁡max⁡{|FPN​(σ,z)|,ε}​d​md​(z).\displaystyle\quad=\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\log\max\{|F_{P_{N}}(\sigma,z)|,\varepsilon\}\,\mathrm{d}m_{d}(z). (33)

This is the finite-integral-base spatial extension used by Jessen and Tornehave [12, §116].

For 0<ε≤10<\varepsilon\leq 1,

|log⁡max⁡{|FPN|,ε}|≤log+⁡‖FPN‖∞+log−⁡|FPN|.\left|\log\max\{|F_{P_{N}}|,\varepsilon\}\right|\leq\log^{+}\|F_{P_{N}}\|_{\infty}+\log^{-}|F_{P_{N}}|.

The right-hand side is integrable by Lemma 3.2. Hence dominated convergence gives

limε↓0∫𝕋dlog⁡max⁡{|FPN​(σ,z)|,ε}​d​md​(z)=∫𝕋dlog⁡|FPN​(σ,z)|​d​md​(z).\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\log\max\{|F_{P_{N}}(\sigma,z)|,\varepsilon\}\,\mathrm{d}m_{d}(z)=\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\log|F_{P_{N}}(\sigma,z)|\,\mathrm{d}m_{d}(z).

Combining this with (33) and [12, Theorem 5] proves (32). Finiteness follows from Lemma 3.2, while convexity follows from Jessen and Tornehave [12, Theorem 7]. ∎

3.3 Jessen–Tornehave zero density

For a convex function JJ, write J′​(x−)J^{\prime}(x-) and J′​(x+)J^{\prime}(x+) for its left and right derivatives.

Proposition 3.4 (Vertical zero density).

Let Z⁡(PN)Z(P_{N}) denote the multiset of zeros ρ=β+i​γ\rho=\beta+i\gamma of PNP_{N}. If a<ba<b, then the vertical zero frequency in the strip a<Re⁡s<ba<\operatorname{Re}s<b exists and

limT→∞12​T#{ρ∈Z(PN):a<β<b,|γ|<T}=12​π(JPN′(b−)−JPN′(a+)).\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2T}\#\{\rho\in Z(P_{N}):a<\beta<b,\ |\gamma|<T\}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\bigl(J_{P_{N}}^{\prime}(b-)-J_{P_{N}}^{\prime}(a+)\bigr). (34)

Equivalently,

ρPN:=12​π​JPN′′\rho_{P_{N}}:=\frac{1}{2\pi}J_{P_{N}}^{\prime\prime} (35)

is the locally finite vertical zero-density measure on the real axis.

Proof.

This is Jessen and Tornehave [12, Theorem 31], applied to the ordinary Dirichlet series PNP_{N}. Their Jensen function is

φ⁡(σ):=limT→∞12​T​∫−TTlog⁡|PN​(σ+i​t)|​𝑑t,\varphi(\sigma):=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^{T}\log|P_{N}(\sigma+it)|\,\mathrm{d}t,

so in our notation φ=JPN\varphi=J_{P_{N}}. Theorem 31 gives, for every a<ba<b,

H⁡(a,b)=12​π​(φ′​(b−0)−φ′​(a+0)),H(a,b)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\bigl(\varphi^{\prime}(b-0)-\varphi^{\prime}(a+0)\bigr),

where H⁡(a,b)H(a,b) denotes the relative frequency of zeros in the strip a<Re⁡s<ba<\operatorname{Re}s<b. This is exactly (34). ∎

Remark 3.5.

For f⁡(s)=1+e−λ​sf(s)=1+e^{-\lambda s},

Jf​(σ)=max⁡{0,−λ​σ},Jf′′=λ​δ0.J_{f}(\sigma)=\max\{0,-\lambda\sigma\},\qquad J_{f}^{\prime\prime}=\lambda\delta_{0}.

The zeros are s=(2​m+1)​π​i/λs=(2m+1)\pi i/\lambda, whose vertical density in |Im⁡s|<T|\operatorname{Im}s|<T is λ/(2​π)\lambda/(2\pi). Thus (35) has the correct constant.

3.4 Elementary bounds and total mass

Proposition 3.6.

Assume a1=1a_{1}=1. Then for every σ∈ℝ\sigma\in\mathbb{R},

0≤JPN​(σ)≤12​log​∑n≤N|an|2​n−2​σ.0\leq J_{P_{N}}(\sigma)\leq\frac{1}{2}\log\sum_{n\leq N}|a_{n}|^{2}n^{-2\sigma}. (36)

For the upper bound, use Jensen’s inequality for the concave function x↦log⁡xx\mapsto\log x: if μ\mu is a probability measure and X>0X>0 is integrable, then

∫logXdμ≤log∫Xdμ.\int\log X\,\mathrm{d}\mu\leq\log\int X\,\mathrm{d}\mu.

JPN​(σ)\displaystyle J_{P_{N}}(\sigma) =12​∫𝕋dlog⁡|FPN​(σ,z)|2​d​md​(z)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\log|F_{P_{N}}(\sigma,z)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}m_{d}(z)
≤12​log​∫𝕋d|FPN​(σ,z)|2​d​md​(z).\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\log\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}|F_{P_{N}}(\sigma,z)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}m_{d}(z).

∫𝕋d|FPN​(σ,z)|2​d​md​(z)=∑n≤N|an|2​n−2​σ.\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}|F_{P_{N}}(\sigma,z)|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}m_{d}(z)=\sum_{n\leq N}|a_{n}|^{2}n^{-2\sigma}.

Q⁡(z)=c0+c1​z+⋯+cm​zm=cm​∏j=1m(z−αj),Q(z)=c_{0}+c_{1}z+\cdots+c_{m}z^{m}=c_{m}\prod_{j=1}^{m}(z-\alpha_{j}),

then

∫𝕋log⁡|Q⁡(z)|​𝑑m​(z)=log⁡|cm|+∑j=1mlog+|αj|≥log⁡|c0|,\int_{\mathbb{T}}\log|Q(z)|\,\mathrm{d}m(z)=\log|c_{m}|+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\log^{+}|\alpha_{j}|\geq\log|c_{0}|,

where the last inequality is the equivalent form obtained from |c0|=|cm|​∏j|αj||c_{0}|=|c_{m}|\prod_{j}|\alpha_{j}|. Apply this successively to the variables zd,zd−1,…,z1z_{d},z_{d-1},\ldots,z_{1}. Fubini is legitimate by Lemma 3.2. At each step the circle mean is bounded below by the logarithm of the modulus of the constant coefficient in that variable, and after all variables have been integrated only the constant monomial remains. JPN​(σ)=∫𝕋dlog⁡|FPN​(σ,z)|​d​md​(z)≥log⁡|a1|=0.J_{P_{N}}(\sigma)=\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\log|F_{P_{N}}(\sigma,z)|\,\mathrm{d}m_{d}(z)\geq\log|a_{1}|=0.

Proposition 3.7.

JPN′′​(ℝ)=log⁡MN,ρPN​(ℝ)=log⁡MN2​π.J_{P_{N}}^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{R})=\log M_{N},\qquad\rho_{P_{N}}(\mathbb{R})=\frac{\log M_{N}}{2\pi}. (37)

FPN​(σ,z)=aMN​MN−σ​z𝐯⁡(MN)​(1+o⁡(1)),F_{P_{N}}(\sigma,z)=a_{M_{N}}M_{N}^{-\sigma}z^{\mathbf{v}(M_{N})}(1+o(1)),

ρPN​(ℝ)=12​π​JPN′′​(ℝ)=log⁡MN2​π.\rho_{P_{N}}(\mathbb{R})=\frac{1}{2\pi}J_{P_{N}}^{\prime\prime}(\mathbb{R})=\frac{\log M_{N}}{2\pi}.

A Steinhaus random variable is, by definition, a random variable distributed according to normalized Haar measure on the unit circle 𝕋\mathbb{T}; see, for example, Kahane [13, Chapter 1].

The Bessel function of the first kind of order zero is

J0​(u):=∑n=0∞(−1)n(n!)2​(u2)2​n.J_{0}(u):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}}{(n!)^{2}}\left(\frac{u}{2}\right)^{2n}. (38)

and the classical large-argument expansion implies J0(u)=O(u−1/2)J_{0}(u)=O(u^{-1/2}) as u→+∞u\to+\infty; see Watson [25, §§2.11, 2.2 and 7.21].

Remark 4.2.

The uniformity in the translation aa is essential for the application below. After the other torus coordinates are fixed, the isolated prime-coordinate block is translated by a complex number depending on those fixed coordinates, and the estimate must remain uniform in that translation.

5 The abstract isolated-prime criterion

Let PN​(s)=∑n≤Nan​n−sP_{N}(s)=\sum_{n\leq N}a_{n}n^{-s} and let

𝒬N⊂{p​ prime:N/2<p≤N}.\mathcal{Q}_{N}\subset\{p\text{ prime}:N/2<p\leq N\}.

If p∈𝒬Np\in\mathcal{Q}_{N} and n≤Nn\leq N is divisible by pp, then n=pn=p. Thus the Bohr coordinate zpz_{p} occurs only in the linear monomial ap​p−σ​zpa_{p}p^{-\sigma}z_{p}, and

FPN​(σ,z)=AN​(σ,z′)+∑p∈𝒬Nap​p−σ​zp,F_{P_{N}}(\sigma,z)=A_{N}(\sigma,z^{\prime})+\sum_{p\in\mathcal{Q}_{N}}a_{p}p^{-\sigma}z_{p}, (64)

where ANA_{N} is independent of the coordinates indexed by 𝒬N\mathcal{Q}_{N}.

For a finite set 𝒬\mathcal{Q} of prime coordinates, write

where mm is normalized Haar probability measure on 𝕋\mathbb{T}. If 𝒫⁡(N)\mathcal{P}(N) denotes the set of all primes not exceeding NN, set

ℛN:=𝒫⁡(N)∖𝒬N.\mathcal{R}_{N}:=\mathcal{P}(N)\setminus\mathcal{Q}_{N}.

Then the Bohr torus decomposes as

𝕋d=𝕋ℛN×𝕋𝒬N,d​md=d​mℛN​d​m𝒬N.\mathbb{T}^{d}=\mathbb{T}^{\mathcal{R}_{N}}\times\mathbb{T}^{\mathcal{Q}_{N}},\qquad\,\mathrm{d}m_{d}=\,\mathrm{d}m_{\mathcal{R}_{N}}\,\,\mathrm{d}m_{\mathcal{Q}_{N}}.
Proposition 5.1 (Isolated-prime lower bound).

Let I⊂ℝI\subset\mathbb{R} be compact. Suppose that there exists KI≥1K_{I}\geq 1 such that

for every σ∈I\sigma\in I and every p,q∈𝒬Np,q\in\mathcal{Q}_{N}, and suppose #​𝒬N≥5\#\mathcal{Q}_{N}\geq 5. Then

JPN​(σ)≥12​log​∑p∈𝒬N|ap|2​p−2​σ−CKI(σ∈I),J_{P_{N}}(\sigma)\geq\frac{1}{2}\log\sum_{p\in\mathcal{Q}_{N}}|a_{p}|^{2}p^{-2\sigma}-C_{K_{I}}\qquad(\sigma\in I), (66)

where CKIC_{K_{I}} is the constant from Lemma 4.1.

Proof.

Fix σ∈I\sigma\in I and fix all torus coordinates not indexed by 𝒬N\mathcal{Q}_{N}. Denote this collection by

FPN​(σ,z′,z𝒬N)=AN​(σ,z′)+∑p∈𝒬Nap​p−σ​zp,F_{P_{N}}(\sigma,z^{\prime},z_{\mathcal{Q}_{N}})=A_{N}(\sigma,z^{\prime})+\sum_{p\in\mathcal{Q}_{N}}a_{p}p^{-\sigma}z_{p},

Combining Theorem 2.4 with Proposition 3.4 gives the direct density formulation.

Corollary 6.1 (Critical-line concentration for ζN\zeta_{N}).

For every ε>0\varepsilon>0,

limN→∞2​πlog⁡NlimT→∞12​T#{ρ=β+iγ:ζN(ρ)=0,|β−1/2|≥ε,|γ|<T}=0,\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{2\pi}{\log N}\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2T}\#\left\{\rho=\beta+i\gamma:\zeta_{N}(\rho)=0,\ |\beta-1/2|\geq\varepsilon,\ |\gamma|<T\right\}=0, (84)

with the usual convention of avoiding boundary lines carrying zero frequency.

Remark 6.2.

Corollary 6.1 does not imply that all zeros approach Re⁡s=1/2\operatorname{Re}s=1/2. Mora’s theorem [18] shows that, for sufficiently large fixed NN, real parts of zeros are dense throughout the admissible critical strip. The two statements are compatible: Mora describes support, whereas (84) describes normalized vertical mass.

Proof of Theorem 2.5.

Lemma 7.1 verifies hypothesis (H1) with α=1/2\alpha=1/2.

Let 𝒫N\mathcal{P}_{N} be the dyadic prime set defined in (79). For N>2​qN>2q and p∈𝒫Np\in\mathcal{P}_{N}, one has p>qp>q and hence p∤qp\nmid q, so |χ⁡(p)|=1|\chi(p)|=1. Among any qq consecutive integers there is an integer congruent to 11 modulo qq, hence coprime to qq. Therefore

N−q+1≤MN,χ≤N,N-q+1\leq M_{N,\chi}\leq N, (91)

log⁡MN,χlog⁡N⟶1.\frac{\log M_{N,\chi}}{\log N}\longrightarrow 1.

Remark 7.2.

The argument makes no distinction between principal and nonprincipal characters. In particular, the pole of the limiting principal LL-function at s=1s=1 has no effect on the vertical mean-motion exponent of its finite truncations.

8 Holomorphic modular forms

Let ff be the fixed primitive holomorphic Hecke eigenform introduced in Section 2: it has even weight k≥2k\geq 2, fixed level QQ, trivial Dirichlet character, and no complex multiplication. Its normalized coefficients are λf(n)=af(n)n−(k−1)/2\lambda_{f}(n)=a_{f}(n)n^{-(k-1)/2}.

8.1 Rankin–Selberg quadratic energy

The classical Rankin–Selberg theorem of Rankin [19] and Selberg [24] gives

Af​(x):=∑n≤x|λf​(n)|2=cf​x+Of​(x3/5),cf>0.A_{f}(x):=\sum_{n\leq x}|\lambda_{f}(n)|^{2}=c_{f}x+O_{f}(x^{3/5}),\qquad c_{f}>0. (92)
Lemma 8.1 (Weighted Rankin–Selberg energy).

For fixed σ<1/2\sigma<1/2,

∑n≤N|λf​(n)|2​n−2​σ=cf1−2​σ​N1−2​σ+of,σ​(N1−2​σ).\sum_{n\leq N}|\lambda_{f}(n)|^{2}n^{-2\sigma}=\frac{c_{f}}{1-2\sigma}N^{1-2\sigma}+o_{f,\sigma}(N^{1-2\sigma}). (93)

At σ=1/2\sigma=1/2,

∑n≤N|λf​(n)|2n=cf​log⁡N+Of​(1),\sum_{n\leq N}\frac{|\lambda_{f}(n)|^{2}}{n}=c_{f}\log N+O_{f}(1), (94)

and for σ>1/2\sigma>1/2 the weighted partial sums remain bounded.

Proof.

For σ≠0\sigma\neq 0, Abel summation gives

∑n≤N|λf​(n)|2​n−2​σ=Af​(N)​N−2​σ+2​σ​∫1NAf​(x)​x−2​σ−1​𝑑x.\sum_{n\leq N}|\lambda_{f}(n)|^{2}n^{-2\sigma}=A_{f}(N)N^{-2\sigma}+2\sigma\int_{1}^{N}A_{f}(x)x^{-2\sigma-1}\,\mathrm{d}x. (95)

Insert (92). The contribution of the main term cf​xc_{f}x is

cf​N1−2​σ+2​σ​cf​∫1Nx−2​σ​𝑑x\displaystyle c_{f}N^{1-2\sigma}+2\sigma c_{f}\int_{1}^{N}x^{-2\sigma}\,\mathrm{d}x =cf​N1−2​σ+2​σ​cf1−2​σ​(N1−2​σ−1)\displaystyle=c_{f}N^{1-2\sigma}+\frac{2\sigma c_{f}}{1-2\sigma}(N^{1-2\sigma}-1)
=cf1−2​σ​N1−2​σ+Of,σ​(1).\displaystyle=\frac{c_{f}}{1-2\sigma}N^{1-2\sigma}+O_{f,\sigma}(1).

The contribution of the error Of​(x3/5)O_{f}(x^{3/5}) is

Of(N3/5−2​σ)+Of,σ(∫1Nx−2/5−2σdx).O_{f}(N^{3/5-2\sigma})+O_{f,\sigma}\left(\int_{1}^{N}x^{-2/5-2\sigma}\,\mathrm{d}x\right). (96)

The first term divided by N1−2​σN^{1-2\sigma} is Of(N−2/5)O_{f}(N^{-2/5}). For the integral term there are three cases:

∫1Nx−2/5−2σdx={Oσ​(N3/5−2​σ),σ<3/10,O⁡(log⁡N),σ=3/10,Oσ​(1),3/10<σ<1/2.\int_{1}^{N}x^{-2/5-2\sigma}\,\mathrm{d}x=\begin{cases}O_{\sigma}(N^{3/5-2\sigma}),&\sigma<3/10,\\ O(\log N),&\sigma=3/10,\\ O_{\sigma}(1),&3/10<\sigma<1/2.\end{cases}

After division by N1−2​σN^{1-2\sigma} these are respectively O(N−2/5)O(N^{-2/5}), O(N−2/5logN)O(N^{-2/5}\log N), and O⁡(N−(1−2​σ))O(N^{-(1-2\sigma)}), all tending to zero. This proves (93); the case σ=0\sigma=0 follows directly from (92).

At σ=1/2\sigma=1/2, partial summation yields

∑n≤N|λf​(n)|2n\displaystyle\sum_{n\leq N}\frac{|\lambda_{f}(n)|^{2}}{n} =Af​(N)N+∫1NAf​(x)x2​𝑑x\displaystyle=\frac{A_{f}(N)}{N}+\int_{1}^{N}\frac{A_{f}(x)}{x^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x
=cf+Of(N−2/5)+cf∫1Nd​xx+Of(∫1Nx−7/5dx)\displaystyle=c_{f}+O_{f}(N^{-2/5})+c_{f}\int_{1}^{N}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}x}{x}+O_{f}\left(\int_{1}^{N}x^{-7/5}\,\mathrm{d}x\right)
=cf​log⁡N+Of​(1),\displaystyle=c_{f}\log N+O_{f}(1),

proving (94). Finally, if σ>1/2\sigma>1/2, then Af(x)≪fxA_{f}(x)\ll_{f}x, and the same partial-summation formula shows that the infinite series ∑n≥1|λf​(n)|2​n−2​σ\sum_{n\geq 1}|\lambda_{f}(n)|^{2}n^{-2\sigma} converges. ∎

It follows from Lemma 8.1 that

12​log⁡N​log​∑n≤N|λf​(n)|2​n−2​σ⟶(12−σ)+.\frac{1}{2\log N}\log\sum_{n\leq N}|\lambda_{f}(n)|^{2}n^{-2\sigma}\longrightarrow\left(\frac{1}{2}-\sigma\right)_{+}. (97)

8.2 Sato–Tate and isolated prime coordinates

Let p∤Qp\nmid Q be prime. The Ramanujan–Petersson theorem for holomorphic forms, proved by Deligne [6], gives |af​(p)|≤2​p(k−1)/2|a_{f}(p)|\leq 2p^{(k-1)/2}. Because the Dirichlet character is trivial, the normalized Hecke eigenvalue λf​(p)\lambda_{f}(p) is real. Hence there is an angle θp∈[0,π]\theta_{p}\in[0,\pi] such that

λf(p)=2cosθp.\lambda_{f}(p)=2\cos\theta_{p}. (98)

Since ff has no complex multiplication, the Sato–Tate theorem [2, Corollary 7.1.7] states that the angles θp\theta_{p}, over unramified primes, are equidistributed on [0,π][0,\pi] with respect to

d​μST​(θ)=2π​sin2⁡θ​d​θ.\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{\mathrm{ST}}(\theta)=\frac{2}{\pi}\sin^{2}\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta. (99)

Equivalently, the values λf(p)=2cosθp\lambda_{f}(p)=2\cos\theta_{p} are distributed on [−2,2][-2,2] according to the semicircle measure

d​νST​(x)=12​π​4−x2​d​x.\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{\mathrm{ST}}(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{4-x^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x. (100)

Let

𝒜:={x∈[−2,2]:1≤|x|≤2},η:=νST​(𝒜)>0.\mathcal{A}:=\{x\in[-2,2]:1\leq|x|\leq 2\},\qquad\eta:=\nu_{\mathrm{ST}}(\mathcal{A})>0.

The boundary of 𝒜\mathcal{A} has νST\nu_{\mathrm{ST}}-measure zero. Therefore [2, Corollary 7.1.7] gives

#{p≤x:p∤Q, 1≤|λf(p)|≤2}=ηπ(x)+o(π(x)).\#\{p\leq x:p\nmid Q,\ 1\leq|\lambda_{f}(p)|\leq 2\}=\eta\,\pi(x)+o(\pi(x)). (101)

Applying this at x=Nx=N and x=N/2x=N/2, and using the prime number theorem, yields

#{N/2<p≤N:p∤Q, 1≤|λf(p)|≤2}=(η2+o(1))Nlog⁡N.\#\{N/2<p\leq N:p\nmid Q,\ 1\leq|\lambda_{f}(p)|\leq 2\}=\left(\frac{\eta}{2}+o(1)\right)\frac{N}{\log N}. (102)

Define

𝒫N,f:={p:N/2<p≤N,p∤Q, 1≤|λf(p)|≤2}.\mathcal{P}_{N,f}:=\{p:N/2<p\leq N,\ p\nmid Q,\ 1\leq|\lambda_{f}(p)|\leq 2\}. (103)

Then #​𝒫N,f→∞\#\mathcal{P}_{N,f}\to\infty.

Let I⊂ℝI\subset\mathbb{R} be compact and put MI:=maxτ∈I⁡|τ|M_{I}:=\max_{\tau\in I}|\tau|. If p,r∈𝒫N,fp,r\in\mathcal{P}_{N,f} and σ∈I\sigma\in I, then 1≤|λf​(p)|,|λf​(r)|≤21\leq|\lambda_{f}(p)|,|\lambda_{f}(r)|\leq 2 and 1/2<p/r<21/2<p/r<2. Hence

12MI+1≤|λf​(p)|​p−σ|λf​(r)|​r−σ≤2MI+1.\frac{1}{2^{M_{I}+1}}\leq\frac{|\lambda_{f}(p)|p^{-\sigma}}{|\lambda_{f}(r)|r^{-\sigma}}\leq 2^{M_{I}+1}. (104)

Thus the isolated weights are uniformly comparable. Moreover, for σ<1/2\sigma<1/2,

BN,f​(σ)\displaystyle B_{N,f}(\sigma) :=∑p∈𝒫N,f|λf​(p)|2​p−2​σ.\displaystyle:=\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{N,f}}|\lambda_{f}(p)|^{2}p^{-2\sigma}. (105)

Since 1≤|λf​(p)|2≤41\leq|\lambda_{f}(p)|^{2}\leq 4 and N/2<p≤NN/2<p\leq N,

2−2​|σ|N−2​σ#𝒫N,f≪σBN,f(σ)≪σN−2​σ#𝒫N,f.2^{-2|\sigma|}N^{-2\sigma}\#\mathcal{P}_{N,f}\ll_{\sigma}B_{N,f}(\sigma)\ll_{\sigma}N^{-2\sigma}\#\mathcal{P}_{N,f}.

Together with (102), this gives

BN,f​(σ)=N1−2​σ+o⁡(1),B_{N,f}(\sigma)=N^{1-2\sigma+o(1)}, (106)

with the o⁡(1)o(1) uniform for σ\sigma in compact subsets of (−∞,1/2)(-\infty,1/2). Hence

12​log⁡N​log⁡BN,f​(σ)⟶12−σ\frac{1}{2\log N}\log B_{N,f}(\sigma)\longrightarrow\frac{1}{2}-\sigma (107)

locally uniformly on (−∞,1/2)(-\infty,1/2).

8.3 Proof of the modular theorem

Proof of Theorem 2.6.

Equation (97) verifies hypothesis (H1) with α=1/2\alpha=1/2. Taking the abstract set 𝒬N\mathcal{Q}_{N} to be 𝒫N,f\mathcal{P}_{N,f}, equations (104) and (107) verify hypothesis (H2).

By (102), for all sufficiently large NN there is a prime p∈(N/2,N]p\in(N/2,N] with λf​(p)≠0\lambda_{f}(p)\neq 0. Consequently

N/2<MN,f≤N,log⁡MN,flog⁡N⟶1.N/2<M_{N,f}\leq N,\qquad\frac{\log M_{N,f}}{\log N}\longrightarrow 1.

Theorem 2.2 now gives (21) and (22).

Finally, from af​(n)=λf​(n)​n(k−1)/2a_{f}(n)=\lambda_{f}(n)n^{(k-1)/2},

ℒN​(s,f)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{N}(s,f) =∑n≤Naf​(n)​n−s\displaystyle=\sum_{n\leq N}a_{f}(n)n^{-s}
=∑n≤Nλf​(n)​n−(s−(k−1)/2)\displaystyle=\sum_{n\leq N}\lambda_{f}(n)n^{-(s-(k-1)/2)}
=LN​(s−k−12,f).\displaystyle=L_{N}\left(s-\frac{k-1}{2},f\right). (108)

Thus the real parts of all zeros are translated by (k−1)/2(k-1)/2, and the concentration line Re⁡w=1/2\operatorname{Re}w=1/2 in the normalized variable w=s−(k−1)/2w=s-(k-1)/2 becomes

Re⁡s=12+k−12=k2.\operatorname{Re}s=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{k-1}{2}=\frac{k}{2}.

∎

Corollary 8.2.

In particular, Theorem 2.6 applies to every normalized holomorphic Hecke cusp eigenform for SL2​(ℤ)\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z}). Zero-density concentration occurs on Re⁡s=1/2\operatorname{Re}s=1/2 for the normalized Hecke-eigenvalue truncations and on Re⁡s=k/2\operatorname{Re}s=k/2 for the classical Fourier-coefficient truncations.

9 Conclusion

We have proved a general criterion that converts quadratic coefficient growth, together with a sufficiently large family of isolated prime coordinates, into concentration of normalized vertical zero density on a single line. The Bohr–Jessen identity turns the vertical logarithmic mean into a torus Mahler measure, while the translation-uniform Steinhaus estimate prevents the isolated linear block from spending excessive Haar measure near zero. The resulting lower bound matches the elementary L2L^{2} upper bound at logarithmic scale.

The limiting potential is

Vα​(σ)=(α−σ)+,V_{\alpha}(\sigma)=(\alpha-\sigma)_{+},

whose unique corner gives Vα′′=δαV_{\alpha}^{\prime\prime}=\delta_{\alpha}. For the partial sums of the Riemann zeta function and of fixed Dirichlet LL-functions, α=1/2\alpha=1/2. Rankin–Selberg and Sato–Tate give the same value for normalized holomorphic Hecke eigenforms of fixed level without complex multiplication; in the classical Fourier-coefficient normalization the corresponding line is Re⁡s=k/2\operatorname{Re}s=k/2.
The present argument is intrinsically formulated in the Jessen mean-motion regime, with T→∞T\to\infty for each fixed NN before N→∞N\to\infty. A coupled (N,T)(N,T) limit would require quantitative control of the passage from vertical averages to Haar averages that is uniform in the growing frequency set {log⁡p:p≤N}\{\log p:p\leq N\}, and no such uniform estimate is used here.

The conclusion is compatible with the much wider support of individual zeros for a fixed truncation: concentration of normalized vertical density is a measure-theoretic statement and does not assert geometric concentration of the entire zero set.
